title: HTTP Methods & Status Codes: The Field Manual
summary: A dense study-notes handbook on HTTP request methods and response status codes — what safe, idempotent, and cacheable really mean, how every status family behaves on the wire, and how to pick the exact right code for each situation.

chapters.title: HTTP Request Basics: Anatomy of a Method
points: An HTTP request line is `METHOD SP request-target SP HTTP-version` — e.g. `GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1`
Methods are case-sensitive and always uppercase by convention; `get` is not `GET` and servers must reject it
The method is the *semantic verb*: it tells the server what the client intends, not how the server implements it
The standard method set: GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS, TRACE, CONNECT
GET retrieves a representation of the target resource; it is the only method a browser address bar issues
HEAD is GET without a body — identical headers, including `Content-Length`, so you can size a resource before downloading
POST submits data to be processed by the target resource; the server decides what to create and where
PUT replaces the entire target resource with the enclosed representation; the client picks the URL
PATCH applies a partial modification described by a patch document (JSON Patch RFC 6902, JSON Merge Patch RFC 7386)
DELETE requests removal of the target resource
OPTIONS asks what the resource supports; the response carries an `Allow:` header, and it drives CORS preflight
TRACE echoes the request back for loopback debugging — disabled almost everywhere because of Cross-Site Tracing (XST)
CONNECT opens a TCP tunnel through a proxy, used for HTTPS via HTTP proxies
Not every method is defined for every resource — 405 Method Not Allowed exists for exactly this case
Extension methods are legal (WebDAV: PROPFIND, MKCOL, LOCK) but only registered methods get generic handling

chapters.title: Safe, Idempotent, Cacheable: The Three Properties
points: **Safe** = read-only semantics; the request is not intended to change server state. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE
Safe does not mean *zero* side effects — logging, analytics counters, and rate-limit counters are fine; the client just isn't *responsible* for the change
**Idempotent** = making N identical requests has the same effect on server state as making 1. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT, DELETE
Idempotency is about *server state*, not the *response*. `DELETE /users/42` returns 204 then 404 — different responses, same final state, still idempotent
Every safe method is idempotent; the reverse is false — PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe
**Cacheable** = the response may be stored and reused. GET and HEAD by default; POST only when it carries explicit freshness headers; PUT/DELETE/PATCH never
POST is neither safe nor idempotent — that's why the browser shows "Confirm Form Resubmission" on reload
PATCH is not idempotent in general: `{"op":"add","path":"/tags/-","value":"x"}` appends a tag every time
PATCH *can* be idempotent if the patch document is absolute (JSON Merge Patch `{"status":"paid"}` is idempotent)
Why it matters: intermediaries, proxies, and HTTP clients automatically retry idempotent requests on connection failure
Why it matters: crawlers and prefetchers follow GET links freely — never hide a destructive action behind a GET
Classic bug: `GET /posts/42/delete` — a link prefetcher or antivirus scanner will silently wipe the database
Quick table — GET: safe✓ idem✓ cache✓ | POST: ✗ ✗ conditional | PUT: ✗ ✓ ✗ | PATCH: ✗ ✗ ✗ | DELETE: ✗ ✓ ✗
`Idempotency-Key: <uuid>` header is the industry pattern (Stripe, PayPal) for making POST safe to retry — server stores the key and replays the first response

chapters.title: GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS in Depth
points: GET must not carry a semantically meaningful body — RFC 9110 says a body "may cause some implementations to reject the request"
Consequence: complex queries go in the query string, or you POST to a `/search` endpoint and accept losing cacheability
URL length is not spec-limited but is practically capped ~2 KB by IE legacy, ~8 KB by nginx `large_client_header_buffers`
Conditional GET: `If-None-Match: "etag"` or `If-Modified-Since: <date>` → 304 Not Modified with no body
Range GET: `Range: bytes=0-1023` → 206 Partial Content with `Content-Range: bytes 0-1023/5000`; enables resumable downloads and video seeking
HEAD must return exactly the headers GET would, and MUST NOT return a body — a server that sends `Content-Length: 0` on HEAD is broken
HEAD uses: link checkers, cache validity probes, checking file size before a big download
OPTIONS on `*` (`OPTIONS * HTTP/1.1`) asks about the server itself, not a resource
CORS preflight is an OPTIONS request carrying `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `Access-Control-Request-Headers`
Preflight response must return `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `-Allow-Headers`, and `Access-Control-Max-Age` to cache the preflight
Preflight is triggered by non-simple methods (PUT/PATCH/DELETE) or non-simple headers (`Authorization`, custom `X-*`, `Content-Type: application/json`)
Gotcha: your OPTIONS handler must return 200 or 204 *without* auth — requiring a token on preflight breaks every browser client
GET response should be idempotent-friendly: never mutate on GET even for "convenience" endpoints like `/api/refresh-cache`

chapters.title: POST vs PUT vs PATCH: Who Owns the URL
points: POST: the *server* decides the resulting URL. `POST /orders` → `201 Created` + `Location: /orders/8812`
PUT: the *client* decides the URL. `PUT /users/42` creates or replaces the resource at exactly that URL
Rule of thumb: if you can't name the URL before the request, it's a POST
PUT is a full replacement — omitted fields are deleted, not preserved. Sending `{"name":"Ada"}` to a user with an email wipes the email
PATCH is partial — only the described fields change
JSON Merge Patch (`Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json`): `{"email":null}` deletes the field, missing keys are untouched
JSON Patch (`application/json-patch+json`): an ordered op array `[{"op":"replace","path":"/email","value":"a@b.c"}]` — expressive but verbose
Never use `Content-Type: application/json` for a PATCH body and expect interop — declare the patch format
PUT to a collection (`PUT /users`) means "replace the entire collection" — almost never what you want
POST is the universal escape hatch for actions that aren't CRUD: `POST /orders/8812/cancel`, `POST /jobs/9/retry`
Concurrency: guard PUT/PATCH with `If-Match: "etag"` → 412 Precondition Failed on conflict, preventing lost updates
Create-only PUT: `If-None-Match: *` succeeds only if the resource doesn't exist yet
Comparison row — POST: create w/ server URL, not idempotent, 201 | PUT: full replace at known URL, idempotent, 200/201/204 | PATCH: partial change, usually not idempotent, 200/204
Common mistake: using POST for everything ("RPC over HTTP") loses caching, retry safety, and intermediary understanding

chapters.title: DELETE, Soft Deletes, and Async Work
points: `DELETE /users/42` requests removal; success is 204 No Content (nothing to return), or 200 with a body describing what was deleted
202 Accepted when deletion is queued — return a `Location` pointing to a status resource the client can poll
Second DELETE returns 404 or 410 — this is correct and still idempotent, since state is unchanged after the first
Some APIs return 204 on repeat DELETE to keep clients simple; both are defensible, but document which you chose
410 Gone vs 404 Not Found: 410 asserts the resource *existed and was intentionally removed*; search engines drop 410 URLs faster
Soft delete (setting `deleted_at`) is a business concept — over HTTP it should still look like a DELETE, not a `POST /users/42/soft-delete`
DELETE with a body is legal in HTTP/1.1 but widely dropped by proxies and unsupported by some clients — never rely on it
Bulk delete has no clean HTTP shape: `DELETE /users?ids=1,2,3` (query-string) or `POST /users/bulk-delete` are the two pragmatic choices
Cascading deletes: return 409 Conflict when the resource has dependents you refuse to remove, and name them in the body
Permission nuance: 403 Forbidden for "you may not delete this", 405 Method Not Allowed for "this resource is never deletable"
405 responses MUST include an `Allow:` header listing what *is* allowed — most frameworks forget this
The long-running-operation pattern: 202 + `Location: /operations/abc` + poll → 200 with status, then 303 See Other to the finished resource
Deleting a cached resource: return `Cache-Control: no-store` on the DELETE and invalidate downstream caches; the 2xx from an unsafe method invalidates the URL in shared caches

chapters.title: Status Code Anatomy and the 1xx/2xx Families
points: Status line: `HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found` — a 3-digit code plus a reason phrase that clients MUST ignore
The first digit is the class; a client that doesn't recognize `418` MUST treat it as `400` — the generic x00 of its class
Five classes: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
100 Continue: client sends `Expect: 100-continue`, waits for the go-ahead before uploading a huge body — saves bandwidth on rejection
101 Switching Protocols: the WebSocket handshake response, with `Upgrade: websocket` and `Connection: Upgrade`
103 Early Hints: sends `Link: </style.css>; rel=preload` before the real response so the browser starts fetching assets early
200 OK: generic success; the body carries the representation. Correct for GET, and for POST/PUT/PATCH when you return the updated entity
201 Created: a new resource exists; MUST include `Location:` with its URL. Body usually contains the created representation
202 Accepted: request valid and queued, but not yet performed — the outcome is not guaranteed
204 No Content: success, and there is deliberately no body. Correct for DELETE and for PUT/PATCH when the client already knows the state
204 vs 200-with-empty-body: 204 tells the client not to expect a body at all; a 200 with `Content-Length: 0` is wasteful and confuses some clients
205 Reset Content: tells the client to clear the form it submitted — rare, but exists
206 Partial Content: the answer to a `Range` request; pairs with `Accept-Ranges: bytes` on the full response
Gotcha: a 204 MUST NOT include a message body or `Content-Length` — some servers emit both and break HTTP/1.1 keep-alive parsing
Gotcha: returning 200 with `{"error": "..."}` in the body defeats every generic client, proxy, monitor, and retry policy you will ever use

chapters.title: 3xx Redirection: Permanence and Method Rewriting
points: 301 Moved Permanently: the resource has a new canonical URL; clients and search engines should update links
302 Found: a temporary redirect — historically the most misused code in HTTP
The 302 problem: the spec said "keep the method", but every browser rewrote POST to GET, so RFC 7231 split the semantics
303 See Other: *always* switch to GET for the target. This is the correct POST-Redirect-GET code
307 Temporary Redirect: same as 302 but MUST preserve the method and body — POST stays POST
308 Permanent Redirect: same as 301 but MUST preserve the method and body
Cheat sheet — permanent+rewrite: 301 | temporary+rewrite: 302/303 | temporary+preserve: 307 | permanent+preserve: 308
POST-Redirect-GET (PRG): POST the form → 303 → browser GETs the result page, so refresh doesn't resubmit
304 Not Modified: not really a redirect — it means "your cached copy is still valid". No body; MUST include the validators (`ETag`)
304 is emitted in response to conditional requests (`If-None-Match`, `If-Modified-Since`), and saves the entire payload
300 Multiple Choices and 305 Use Proxy (deprecated, security hazard) are effectively dead codes
Browsers and caches remember 301/308 aggressively — a wrong permanent redirect can persist in users' browsers for months. Test with 302 first
HTTPS upgrade should be 301 to the canonical `https://` origin, paired with HSTS (`Strict-Transport-Security`)
Redirect loops: clients cap at ~20 hops then error; a mismatched trailing-slash rule between your app and load balancer is the usual cause

chapters.title: 4xx Client Errors: Say Exactly What's Wrong
points: 400 Bad Request: the request is malformed — unparseable JSON, missing required field, invalid syntax. The generic 4xx fallback
401 Unauthorized: actually means *unauthenticated*. MUST include `WWW-Authenticate:` naming the scheme (e.g. `Bearer realm="api"`)
403 Forbidden: authenticated, identity understood, but not permitted. Re-authenticating will not help
401 vs 403 in one line: 401 = "who are you?", 403 = "I know who you are, and no"
404 Not Found: no representation at this URL. Also the correct answer when you want to hide a resource's existence from an unauthorized caller
405 Method Not Allowed: the URL exists but the method doesn't apply. MUST send `Allow: GET, POST`
406 Not Acceptable: no representation matches the `Accept:` header. Rare — most servers just return their default format instead
409 Conflict: the request conflicts with current state — a duplicate unique key, an edit against a stale version, deleting a parent with children
410 Gone: intentionally and permanently removed; more informative than 404 when you know the history
412 Precondition Failed: an `If-Match`/`If-Unmodified-Since` guard didn't hold — the optimistic-locking failure code
413 Content Too Large, 414 URI Too Long, 415 Unsupported Media Type (wrong `Content-Type`, e.g. sending XML to a JSON-only endpoint)
422 Unprocessable Content: syntactically valid but semantically wrong — well-formed JSON, but `age: -5`. The validation-error workhorse
429 Too Many Requests: rate limited. SHOULD include `Retry-After: 60` (seconds or HTTP-date) and ideally `RateLimit-*` headers
400 vs 422 debate: use 400 for "I can't parse this", 422 for "I parsed it and the values are wrong"; pick one convention and hold it API-wide
RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` is the standard error body: `{type, title, status, detail, instance}` — stop inventing a bespoke error envelope

chapters.title: 5xx Server Errors, Retries, and Resilience
points: 500 Internal Server Error: an unhandled exception. It is *your* fault and it is not actionable by the client
502 Bad Gateway: a proxy or load balancer got an invalid response from upstream — the app crashed or returned garbage
503 Service Unavailable: temporarily down — overloaded, deploying, or in maintenance. SHOULD include `Retry-After`
504 Gateway Timeout: upstream didn't answer in time. Distinct from 502: the connection worked, the clock ran out
501 Not Implemented: the server doesn't recognize the method at all — a server-wide statement, unlike 405 which is per-resource
505 HTTP Version Not Supported, 507 Insufficient Storage (WebDAV), 511 Network Authentication Required (captive portals)
Never leak stack traces, SQL, or file paths in a 5xx body; return a correlation ID (`{"trace_id":"abc123"}`) and log the rest server-side
Retry rules: retry 502/503/504 and connection errors; do NOT blindly retry 500 (the write may have already committed)
Retry only idempotent methods automatically. For POST, require an `Idempotency-Key` before retrying
Backoff: exponential with full jitter — `sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))`. Fixed-interval retries cause thundering herds
Honor `Retry-After` when present; it overrides your backoff calculation
Circuit breaker: after N consecutive 5xx, open the circuit and fail fast for a cooldown, then half-open with a probe request
499 (nginx, non-standard) means the client closed the connection before a response — usually your endpoint is too slow, not an error
Health checks should return 200 only when dependencies are actually reachable; a shallow `return 200` health check hides every real outage
Alerting rule of thumb: 4xx rate is a *client contract* signal, 5xx rate is a *pager* signal

chapters.title: Choosing the Right Code: Decision Rules & Cheat Sheet
points: Decision walk: Did the server break? → 5xx. Did the client break? → 4xx. Do they need to go elsewhere? → 3xx. Otherwise 2xx
Within 2xx: created something new → 201+`Location` | queued for later → 202 | nothing to return → 204 | otherwise → 200
Within 4xx: unparseable → 400 | not logged in → 401 | logged in, not allowed → 403 | no such URL → 404 | wrong verb → 405 | state clash → 409 | bad values → 422 | too fast → 429
Create flow: `POST /articles` → 201, `Location: /articles/77`, body = the created article
Update flow: `PUT /articles/77` with `If-Match` → 200 (returning entity) or 204 (client already has it); 412 if the ETag is stale
Delete flow: `DELETE /articles/77` → 204; repeat call → 404 or 410; blocked by dependents → 409
Login flow: bad password → 401 (not 403, not 200-with-error); too many attempts → 429 with `Retry-After`
Validation flow: malformed JSON → 400; valid JSON with `email: "nope"` → 422 + `problem+json` listing the failed fields
Async flow: `POST /reports` → 202 + `Location: /jobs/5` → poll `GET /jobs/5` → 200 running → 303 See Other to `/reports/91` when finished
Anti-pattern: 200 for everything with a `success: false` body — breaks monitoring, caching, retries, and every HTTP-aware tool
Anti-pattern: 500 for validation errors — pages your on-call engineer for a user's typo
Anti-pattern: 401 when you meant 403, so clients loop forever re-authenticating with a token that was never the problem
Anti-pattern: 302 after a POST when you meant 303 or 307 — the method silently changes and the body is lost
Testing checklist: assert the *status code* in tests, not just the body; a route that returns 200 instead of 201 breaks client contracts silently
Closing rule: the status code is the API's protocol-level answer; the body is the human-level detail. Get the code right first, then explain in `problem+json`
